content.text:
The AIRCoder paper checks out ([ACL 2026](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.1166/)): it scores code with several retrieval methods at once and learns how much to trust each one per query, which it reports as 10.2× more efficient than other methods.

Before the design, one important point: **4 of these 6 papers solve a different problem from ours.** AIRCoder, Repoformer, CodeRAG and RepoCoder are about code completion, meaning predicting the next lines at a cursor. Our problem is an agent finding which files to fix. Their ideas still transfer, but not their systems. RepoGraph and CodePlan are about agents and multi-file edits, which is exactly where our test failed.

## What we take from each paper

| Paper | Idea we take | What we skip and why |
|---|---|---|
| **RepoGraph** | A code graph (definitions, references, imports), and show the agent a symbol's neighbourhood: what it uses and what uses it | Nothing major; this is the core |
| **CodePlan** | **Change impact:** after an edit, find other code that depends on what changed. This directly fixes the missed second file in our hard bug. | The full planning system; too heavy |
| **AIRCoder** | Mix several retrieval signals (text, symbols, graph) with weights that adapt per query | Its learned fusion model. Start with simple rank fusion, and learn weights later from eval data. |
| **Repoformer** | **Only retrieve when it helps.** That's where most of the cost saving comes from. | Its trained self-check model. Use simple rules instead: free and instant. |
| **CodeRAG** | Retrieve along several paths at once, then rerank | LLM reranking: it costs money and time on every query |
| **RepoCoder** | Retrieve again using what was just learned | Nothing separate: the agent loop already does this, and we hook it after edits |

## The design: 4 layers, cheapest first

```
 Task arrives (e.g. failing tests)
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ L3  Seed + gate (Repoformer)    rule-based, no LLM       │
 │     strong signal? → hand the agent 3–5 likely files     │
 │     weak signal?   → inject nothing (save tokens)        │
 └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ L2  Agent tools                                          │
 │   code_search(query)   multi-path + fusion  (CodeRAG,    │
 │                        AIRCoder)                         │
 │   code_context(symbol) def + callers + callees, compact  │
 │                        (RepoGraph)                       │
 │   impact(edited)       who depends on what changed       │
 │                        (CodePlan)                        │
 │   + existing grep / glob / read                          │
 └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ L1  Code index (RepoGraph)  built once, updated per edit │
 │     symbols · imports · calls · references · paths       │
 │     tree-sitter parse, cached on disk by file hash       │
 └───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                 ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ L0  Precision on demand (LSP, the earlier design)        │
 │     only when the index is ambiguous                     │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### L1: The code index
- **Builds a graph:** it parses every file with tree-sitter (fast, many languages, no language server needed) and records which files define and use which symbols, and which import which.
- **Is cheap to keep fresh:** it's cached by file hash, so only changed files are re-parsed, and the existing `fs/*` events update it after every agent edit.
- **Why not LSP for everything:** a TypeScript server can use 1–2 GB of RAM and take up to a minute to load; a tree-sitter index is roughly tens of MB. That's my estimate, to be measured. LSP is the fallback for the cases tree-sitter can't resolve, such as re-exports and overloads.

### L2: Three new tools
1. **`code_search(query)`:**
   - runs 3 searches at once: text (BM25 over identifiers and paths), symbol-name match, and graph neighbours of anything already seen;
   - merges them with reciprocal rank fusion, which is simple and needs no training;
   - returns about 10 files, each with the reason it matched.
2. **`code_context(symbol)`:**
   - returns the definition, its callers, its callees and its imports, one hop out;
   - shows signatures only, not whole files, so the agent reads less.
3. **`impact(files)`:**
   - "You changed X; these files use X." If a function signature or exported type changed, its callers are listed first.

### L3: The seed and the gate
- **Seed from the clues in the task.** At the start, take the stack trace, failing test and error message, look the clues up in the graph, and give the agent 3–5 candidate files, each with its reason.
- **The gate:**
  - Inject the candidates only when the signal is strong, such as a stack trace or a test that clearly imports the code.
  - For vague requests, inject nothing; the agent searches itself.
  - The gate is plain rules, with no LLM call.

### The after-edit loop (RepoCoder and CodePlan)
- **Run `impact` automatically:** after the agent edits a file, `impact` runs on its own. If other files depend on what changed, one short line is added: "3 files reference `close()`: …".
- **This targets our observed failure:** in the hard bug, the agent fixed one file and never touched the dependent file in the other package.
- **A verification nudge:** if the agent says "done" without having run the tests since its last edit, remind it once. That targets the "looks correct" failure.

## Why this beats Claude Code

| | Claude Code (checked in your binary) | This design |
|---|---|---|
| Finding code | grep, glob, read | The same, plus a graph and fused search |
| Symbols | LSP tool, off by default, needs exact line and character | Index queried by symbol name, with LSP as fallback |
| Broad search | Explore subagent (a second model run, costly in tokens) | `code_search` from the index (no LLM call) |
| Start of task | Nothing | Seeded candidates when the signal is strong |
| After an edit | Nothing | Automatic impact check |
| Claiming done | Nothing | One nudge to run the tests |

## Cost and speed

- **No LLM calls in the retrieval path:** no embeddings, no reranker. So retrieval itself costs nothing in tokens and answers in milliseconds.
- **The saving is fewer exploratory reads.** Our hard bug used 67 steps, 29 reads and 4.4M input tokens. Most of that was searching. If seeding and `code_context` cut the reads in half, the token cost roughly halves too.
- **Embeddings can come later, only if measured.** They cost money and time to build and add little for symbol-heavy code; that's my estimate, and the eval would test it.

## Build order, each step gated by the eval

| Step | Adds | Kept only if, on the same tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | L1 index + `code_context` + `impact` | Hard bugs: more right files edited |
| 2 | Seed + gate | Fewer steps and tokens, easy bugs not worse |
| 3 | `code_search` fusion | Fewer reads before the right file |
| 4 | LSP fallback, then learned fusion weights (the full AIRCoder idea) | Measurable accuracy gain |

**First I need more data.** We have only 3 bugs measured, and only 1 shows a file-finding failure. Running about 3 more cross-package bugs first, at about 4M tokens each, would confirm the target before building Step 1.

I can turn this into a shareable design page if you want to show it to others.

Sources:
- [AIRCoder (ACL 2026)](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-long.1166/)
- [RepoCoder (arXiv)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.12570)
- [Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation survey](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.04905)
- [SaraCoder](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.10068)
